recipe.history:
Butternut squash and zucchini are both members of the Cucurbitaceae family, gourds that trace their origins to the Americas — specifically to Mexico and Central America, where they were cultivated by indigenous peoples for thousands of years before European contact. Squash is one of the Three Sisters, the triumvirate of crops — alongside corn and beans — that formed the agricultural backbone of many Native American civilizations. Butternut squash as we know it today, with its characteristic bell shape and sweet, nutty orange flesh, is a relatively recent development, having been developed in the 1940s by Charles Legget of Stow, Massachusetts, who crossed several older squash varieties to create a thin-skinned, sweet-fleshed winter squash that stored exceptionally well. Zucchini, meanwhile, is an Italian-American story: it is a summer squash developed in northern Italy in the 19th century, likely in the Milan region, from squash varieties that had arrived in Europe from the Americas centuries earlier. Both vegetables are deeply tied to harvest time — autumn and late summer — and the flavors they carry are the flavors of that season: sweetness, earthiness, warmth.

The harvest-themed burger is a relatively recent innovation in American cooking, emerging from the farm-to-table movement of the early 2000s when chefs began pushing back against the idea that burgers existed outside of seasonal cooking. Roasted butternut squash, with its caramelized sweetness, turned out to be a remarkable foil for beef — its sugars charring slightly at high heat, its flesh becoming a kind of savory jam that clings to the patty and softens every bite. Zucchini, grilled or pan-fried until tender and slightly blistered, adds a vegetal brightness and a subtle moisture that balances the richness of the beef. Together they make a burger that tastes unmistakably of autumn — of farmers markets and cooling air and the particular satisfaction of cooking with vegetables at the peak of their flavor.

The first time I made a roasted butternut squash spread for a burger, I was trying to use up the last of a fall harvest box that had been sitting on my counter for two weeks. I cubed the squash, tossed it with olive oil, brown sugar, and a little cayenne, and roasted it until it was so soft it practically begged to be mashed. I smeared it on a burger bun on a whim, grilled a few rounds of zucchini in the same pan I'd used for the patty, stacked it all together, and stood at my kitchen counter eating it because I couldn't be bothered to sit down. It was one of those accidental meals that I immediately knew I would make again on purpose. The sweetness of the squash against the savory beef was something I hadn't expected to love as much as I did.

Medium rare is not just a temperature — it is a covenant between the cook and the ingredient. To roast butternut squash until it is caramelized and sweet, to grill zucchini until it is tender and marked, and then to undermine all that careful work by overcooking the beef would be a betrayal. The patty at 130 to 135°F (54 to 57°C) is the anchor of the burger, the element around which all the harvest sweetness orbits. It must be pink, it must be yielding, it must have that mineral richness that only properly cooked beef can offer. Cook it beyond that and you have a dry disc that fights everything around it instead of harmonizing with it.
ingredients: 1.5 lbs (680g) freshly ground beef chuck, 80/20 fat ratio
1 tbsp neutral oil (canola or grapeseed) for cooking
2 tbsp unsalted butter, softened, for toasting buns
For the roasted butternut squash spread:
1 small butternut squash (about 1.5 lbs / 680g), peeled, seeded, and cut into 1-inch cubes
2 medium zucchini, sliced lengthwise into 1/4-inch planks
instructions: 1. Preheat oven to 425°F (220°C). Toss butternut squash cubes with olive oil, brown sugar, cayenne, cinnamon, and salt on a parchment-lined baking sheet. Spread in a single layer and roast for 30–35 minutes, flipping once halfway through, until deeply caramelized and fork-tender.
2. Transfer roasted squash to a bowl. Add butter and apple cider vinegar and mash with a fork until you have a thick, slightly chunky spread. Taste and adjust seasoning. Set aside.
3. Make the herb aioli: stir together mayonnaise, sage, thyme, garlic, and lemon juice. Season with salt and pepper. Refrigerate until ready to use.

4. Brush zucchini planks with olive oil, season with garlic powder, salt, and pepper. Set a grill pan or cast iron skillet over high heat. Grill zucchini for 2–3 minutes per side until tender with distinct grill marks or a golden sear. Transfer to a plate.

5. Divide the ground beef into 4 equal portions (about 6 oz / 170g each). Form each into a patty roughly 3/4 inch thick with a dimple in the center. Season both sides generously with kosher salt and cracked black pepper.
6. Heat neutral oil in a cast iron skillet over high heat until smoking. Add patties and cook undisturbed for 3 minutes.

7. Flip patties, immediately place a slice of white cheddar on each, and cook for 2–2.5 minutes more. Check internal temperature with an instant-read thermometer — pull patties from heat at 130°F (54°C) to reach a final resting temperature of 130–135°F (54–57°C) medium rare.
8. Rest patties on a wire rack, uncovered, for 3–4 minutes.
9. Butter the cut sides of the brioche buns and toast in the skillet over medium heat for 1–2 minutes until golden.

10. Assemble the burgers: spread a generous layer of butternut squash spread on the bottom bun. Add a small handful of arugula, then 2–3 zucchini planks, then the cheesy patty. Sprinkle toasted pumpkin seeds over the patty. Spread herb aioli on the cut side of the top bun, cap the burger, and serve immediately.
